paragraphs: Kechal, shehu haddad shel behema - ben shel qetanna shello hayyeniqa, ben shel gedola – asur middibre soperim lebashshelo – ben bipne atzmo, ben im basar. veim qerao vehotzi hechalab shebbo, muttar litzloto uleakelo: abal lebashshelo, lo day lo biqria, ki ap –al- pi shehotzi hechalab shebbo, mikkol maqom nishar adayin chalab begummot: lepikak im qerao sheti vaereb, vetacho bakkotel ad shello nishar bo lachluchit chalab, muttar min haddin lebashshelo apillu im basar. veim qerao vachatako kamma peamim sheti vaereb al pene kullo - zeh adip tepe mitticha bakkotel. vekol zeh hu middina. abal nahagu berab teputzot yisrael shello lebashshelo im basar kelal, apillu al-yede qeriat sheti vaereb veticha bakkotel, ella mebashshelim oto lebaddo belo basar, o mebashshelim oto im yeraqot ushear debarim sheen bahem basar: veken metaggenim oto lebaddo bemachabat belo basar: veken hamminhag poh irenu bagdad y".veap al gab denahagu shello lebashshelo im basar - im bishshelu im basar, muttar bediabad. kevan deasa lo qeria sheti vaereb veticha bakkotel. veap al gab deyesh omerim deen lehattir bediabad bazeh, el raq behepsed merubbeh - nireh iqqar ledina kehammattirin gam belo hepsed merubbeh. veayyen "peri chadash" v"peri-toar".

clarification.explanation: "Kaveid" (the milk gland of an animal, like an udder) — whether from a young animal that has not yet nursed or from a mature animal — is rabbinically forbidden (not by Torah law) to cook, whether alone or with meat, since it contains milk absorbed within it. If the gland was torn open and the milk removed from it, it is permitted to roast and eat it — but for cooking, tearing alone does not suffice, since even after removing the milk, drops of milk remain within the gland's internal pockets. Therefore, if the gland was torn in two in opposite directions (crosswise) and rubbed against a wall until no moisture of milk remained in it at all, it is Torah-permitted to cook it even with meat. If it was torn and cut several times along its full length, this is even better than rubbing on a wall. All this is by strict law — but in most Jewish communities the custom is to be stringent and not cook the gland with meat at all, even after tearing and rubbing, but to cook it alone or with vegetables and the like containing no meat, and likewise to fry it alone in a pan without meat — and so is the Baghdad custom. But even though the custom is to avoid this, if the gland was actually cooked with meat (after crosswise tearing and rubbing on a wall), it is permitted after the fact, and in practice one may rely on this leniency even without a case of great loss.
takeaways: The milk gland is rabbinically forbidden to cook with meat, unless thoroughly torn (crosswise) and rubbed on a wall to remove all milk moisture.
The accepted custom is to be stringent and not cook the gland with meat at all, but if it was cooked (after tearing and rubbing), it is permitted after the fact even without great loss.

paragraphs: Abar ubishshelo belo qeria: im bishshelo belo basar, ap al pi shebbishshelo im yeraqot ushear debarim, muttar leakelo, vekol - shekken bitzlao belo qeria demuttar bediabad: abal im bishshelo im basar - tzarik keneged kol hakkechal n"t peamim, ki hakkechal atzmo mitztarep: ulekak la baenan shishshim mammash, al saggi betisha vachamishshim sheyyesh babbasar ubishar debarim shebbaqqedera keneged hakkechal, abal hakkechal atzmo, asur, dilma ate lemishre chatikat nebela vegam mishshum hechalab shebbaggummot didda, sheyyesh beoto chalab taam min habbasar shennitbashshel immo: deap al-gab debigmar bishshulo yatza kol hacheleb mimmennu chayeshinan shemma yoklennu qodem gemar bishshulo, vekannizkar bashsha"k za"l. veim lo yesh shishshim, az gam habbasar vehattabshil kullo asurim baakila, abal muttarim bahanaa,lemakeram o letannam legoy, kevan deissuram hu midderabbanan: vehaqqedera tzerika hagala.

clarification.explanation: If one transgressed and cooked the gland without tearing it: if cooked without meat (even with vegetables and other items), it is permitted to eat, and all the more so if roasted without tearing — permitted after the fact. But if cooked with meat, the dish requires a nullification measure of fifty-nine (59) times against the gland, since the gland itself counts toward the quantity needed to nullify it — therefore an ordinary sixty-fold nullification does not suffice; rather fifty-nine parts of meat and the other pot ingredients against the gland suffice. But the gland itself remains forbidden for eating, out of concern one might mistakenly permit a piece of nevelah this way, and also out of concern for the milk in its internal pockets that absorbed taste from the meat cooked with it — since although by the cooking's end all the milk emerges from it, there is concern one might eat the gland before the cooking is fully finished. And if there is no sixty-fold (here, 59) nullification measure in the dish, then the meat and the entire dish are also forbidden for eating — but permitted for benefit, that is, they may be sold or given to a gentile, since the prohibition is only rabbinic. The pot itself requires purging (heat cleaning).
takeaways: Cooking an untorn gland with meat — the dish is permitted only with 59 parts against the gland (the gland itself counts toward the calculation), but the gland itself remains forbidden for eating.
If there is no sufficient nullification measure, the whole dish is forbidden for eating but permitted for benefit (sale, giving to a gentile), and the pot requires purging.

paragraphs: Kechal sheqqerao kedino utzelao, ap -al-pi shemmatza achar-kak gummot meleot chalab, en lachush: mihu, oto hechalab shebbaggummot tzarik leshapeko velo yoklennu, mishshum marit haayin, veken im roeh alayv chalab beayin, yirchatzennu techilla qodem akila, mishshum marit haayin: ken heeleti besipri haqqadosh "mqbtzl". vaayin besiman g, seip , behaggahat-hashshulchan, bedin hakkabed shennitzla verotzeh lebashshelo : vaayin hattaam b"peri chadash" sham, seip qatan v, veken hu hattaam betzali vekannizkar sham, veod besiman v, seip qatan tz.

clarification.explanation: A gland properly torn and roasted, in which pockets full of milk were then found — there is no concern for this by strict law. Nevertheless, the milk found in the pockets should be poured out and not eaten, due to "appearance" (so it does not look as though one is eating milk with meat). Likewise, if visible milk is seen on the gland, it should be washed off before eating, also due to appearance.
takeaways: Milk found in the pockets of a properly torn and roasted gland should be poured out, not eaten, and visible milk should be washed off before eating — all due to appearance, even though by strict law the gland is permitted.

paragraphs: Kechal chay, ap-al-pi shehi melea chalab, muttar lachtok besakkin shel basar, kevan shehu tzonen. veen limloach hakkechal im habbasar, apillu qerao sheti vaereb vetacho bakkotel. ubediabad apillu milcho belo qeria, vaapillu milcho al habbasar, muttar. veayin "erek hashshulchan", avvat z, ushear acharonim.

clarification.explanation: A raw (unbutchered) gland, even though full of milk, may be cut with a meat knife, since it is cold (and does not transfer taste while cold). But the gland should not be salted together with meat, even if it was torn crosswise and rubbed on a wall. However, after the fact, if it was salted without any tearing at all, even salted directly on top of the meat, it is permitted.
takeaways: A raw gland may be cut with a meat knife (since cold), but should not be salted together with meat as the primary practice — if done anyway, permitted after the fact.

paragraphs: Hakkechal, ap-al-pi sheqqerao sheti vaereb vetacho bakkotel, asur litzloto lekattechilla im habbasar, ella tachat habbasar. vaapillu netano bishpud al habbasar, tzarik lahasiro ulehannicho tachat habbasar, vaayin "keneset haggedola", haggahat hattur, ot yd. ubediabad im kebar nitzla, eno neesar. ubeshappudim sheddarkan lehithappek mah shellemala lematta, asur litzloto apillu tachat habbasar, ubediabad muttar. veayin sha"k, seip qatan kh.

clarification.explanation: The gland, even if torn crosswise and rubbed on a wall, may not be roasted as the primary practice together with the meat (on top of it), but should be roasted beneath the meat. Even if placed on the skewer above the meat, it should be moved and placed beneath the meat. After the fact, if it was already roasted above the meat, it does not become forbidden. On skewers that tend to rotate (so that what was on top moves to the bottom), it is forbidden to roast the gland on them at all, even beneath the meat — but after the fact, it is permitted.
takeaways: The gland should always be roasted beneath the meat, not above it; on a rotating skewer it should not be roasted at all as the primary practice — but after the fact, in all cases, it is permitted.

paragraphs: Ap-al-gab deim tzala hakkechal belo qeria sheti vaereb veticha bakkotel, muttar bediabad haynu bitzlao lebaddo, abal im tzelao im basar, asur: sheim natan hakkechal al habbasar, habbasar asur. mishshum shebbala chalab. veim natan hakkechal tachat habbasar, az hakkechal asur, kevan dehabbasar elyon. ubeshappudim sheddarkan lehithappek mah shellemala lematta, shenehem asurim.

clarification.explanation: Although roasting the gland alone without tearing is permitted after the fact, this applies only when it was roasted alone; but if roasted together with meat, it is forbidden: if the gland was placed on top of the meat, the meat itself becomes forbidden, since it absorbed milk from it. And if the gland was placed beneath the meat, then the gland itself becomes forbidden, since it is the meat (above it) that touches and transfers taste to it. On rotating skewers, where the top moves to the bottom, both become forbidden.
takeaways: When roasting the gland with meat together (without prior tearing), the upper piece remains permitted and the lower one becomes forbidden — and on a rotating skewer, both become forbidden.

paragraphs: Or haqqeba leachar shehusar chelbo vehudach, yesh lo din basar mammash, umuttar lemalecho im sheer basar: vehu haddin demuttar lebashshelo, veen lo din kechal kelal: vaayin sha"k veacharonim.

clarification.explanation: The stomach's outer skin (the membrane), once the milk has been removed from it and it has also been thoroughly rinsed, has the law of ordinary meat in every respect, and may be salted together with the rest of the meat. It may likewise be cooked together with meat, and has no law of a milk gland at all.
takeaways: The stomach's skin, once the milk is removed and rinsed, is considered ordinary meat — permitted to salt and cook with meat, with no gland-related law.

paragraphs: Akal basar apillu shel chayya vaop, lo yokal acharayv chalab ad sheyyishheh shesh shaot achar akilato. veap-al-pi shebbechorep hammaakol mitakkel bimhirut yoter memot haqqayitz - gam ken tzarik lehamtin shesh shaot. veim yesh basar ben hashshinnayim tzarik lahasiro: veim lo hesiro tekep achar akila, ella ad achar shettayim veshalosh shaot, en tzarik lachshob hashshesh shaot, ella meet sheggamar akilato: umikkol maqom tzarik leqanneach piv bappat, dehaynu sheyyilas pat veyiblaennu, veachar kak yadicha piv, vekannizkar b"bet yosep", orach-chayyim, siman qg: veayin baacharonim. veap-al-gab dekatebu haacharonim : davqa im matza basar ben hashshinnayim, tzarik lahasiro - abal missetama eno chayyab libdoq: veayyen "keneset haggedola", haggahat hattur, ot y : mikkol maqom, mi sheyyesh lo neqabim beshinnayv, zeh vadday chayyab libdoq, ki chazaqa sheyyesh bahem basar. vehu haddin im akal gebina techilla, veachar-kak rotzeh leekol basar, degam-ken tzarik lechattet,veadam kazeh, tob sheyyargil atzmo lechattet achar kol akila, kede shello yabo lide mikshol: veayyen "shiyyure -beraka" , sop ot kg.

clarification.explanation: One who ate meat, even wild animal or fowl meat, should not eat milk until waiting six hours from finishing the meal. Even in winter, when digestion is faster than in summer, one must still wait a full six hours in the same measure. If there are meat remnants between the teeth, they should be removed; if not removed immediately but only after two or three hours, one need not count six hours from the moment of removal, but from the time the meal ended. In any case one should rinse the mouth with bread (chewing bread and swallowing it) and afterward rinse the mouth with water. Although generally there is no blanket obligation to check between the teeth unless remnants are actually found, one who has cavities in his teeth must check, since it is presumed remnants remain there. The same law applies if one ate cheese first and wants to eat meat afterward — one must also probe and check, and such a person should get into the habit of probing after every meal so as not to stumble.
takeaways: After eating meat, one must wait a full six hours (even in winter) before eating milk, and ensure no meat remnants remain between the teeth — one with dental cavities must check.

paragraphs: Apillu lo akal basar beayin, ki im tabshil shel basar, vaapillu shel op, gam ken tzarik lehamtin shesh shaot kede leekol chalab: vaapillu shata maraq tzalul, gam ken tzarik shesh shaot. veayyen "bet yosep", siman qg, ushear acharonim, v"shiyyure-beraka", kan beyoreh dea ot l. vehalloes lattinoq, name tzarik lehamtin shesh shaot: vaapillu laas tabshil sheyyesh bo shumman dela pelug: abal im taam bilshono upalat miyyad,en tzarik lehamtin. vehu haddin im laqach chatikat basar letok piv, vetekep hecheziro shalem, en tzarik lehamtin: vekol shekken im taam shumman upalat, deen tzarik lehamtin. veayin meheresh qeluger behaggahotayv al "peri megadim", bidpus chadash shel seper "ashle rabrebe".

clarification.explanation: Even one who did not eat actual meat but only a dish containing meat (even fowl meat) must wait six hours before eating milk — even if he only drank a clear broth with a meat taste. One who chews food for an infant (as a preparatory act before feeding him) must likewise wait six hours, even if he chewed a fatty dish — no distinction was made here. But if one only tasted something on the tongue and immediately spat it out, he need not wait. The same law applies if one took a piece of meat into his mouth and immediately took it out whole, without swallowing — he need not wait. And all the more so if one only tasted fat and spat it out — he need not wait.
takeaways: The six-hour waiting obligation also applies to a dish or broth with meat taste, not only actual meat.
A taste immediately spat out without swallowing does not require waiting, but one who chews food for an infant must wait six hours, even if the food is fatty.

paragraphs: Ap-al-gab deamerinan deachar shesh shaot muttar leekol chalab, mikkol maqom baenan name sheyyesalleq hashshulchan sheakal alayv habbasar, vegam sheyyebarek birkat hammazon shel otah seuda: ditlata baenan: shesh shaot, vesilluq shulchan uberaka.veayyen "keneset haggedola", haggaha hattur, ot g. vekamma acharonim veim akal basar belo pat veshulchan, tzarik lebarek beraka acharona, veyishheh shesh shaot.

clarification.explanation: Although after six hours one may eat milk, two additional conditions are also required: clearing the table on which the meat was eaten, and reciting Grace After Meals over that meal. That is, three conditions together: six hours, clearing the table, and Grace After Meals. One who ate meat without bread and without a table must recite the appropriate closing blessing, and wait six hours.
takeaways: Transitioning from meat to milk requires three conditions together: waiting six hours, clearing the table, and reciting Grace After Meals or the appropriate closing blessing over the meat meal.

paragraphs: Letzorek choleh, ap-al-pi sheen bo sakkana, yesh lehaqel lehamtin shaa achat, ak tzarik silluq hashshulchan ubirkat hammazon. veayyen :chakemat-adam" , kelal m, sop ot yg.

clarification.explanation: For a patient, even one not dangerously ill, one may be lenient and wait only one hour instead of six — but the table must still be cleared and Grace After Meals recited.
takeaways: A patient who is not in a dangerous state may be lenient and wait only one hour before eating milk, provided the table is cleared and Grace After Meals is recited.

paragraphs: Tabshil sheen bo basar, veraq beshellevaho biqdera shel basar, apillu hi bat – yoma, hare zeh muttar leekol acharayv chalab miyyad: vaapillu rechitzat yadayim veqinnucha peh en tzarik vaapillu im haqqedera shel habbasar lo huddecha yapeh min tabshil shel habbasar, gam-ken muttar leekol hechalab miyyad. mihu, im lo huddecha yapeh, rauy lehatzrik rechitzat yadayim veqinnucha vahadachat peh,veaz yokal hechalab miyyad: vaayin "shiyyure-beraka" , otiyyot lg v-ld. vehaynu davqa im yesh sheyyasim battabshil hahu keneged likluk haqqedera bebasar, abal im en shishshim keneged likluk habbasar, la saggi lah rechitza veqinnucha vahadachat peh bilbad, ella tzarik lishhot shaa achat lepachot: vehammachmir gam bazeh shesh shaot , tabo alayv beraka. veayin "bet lechem yehuda", seip qatan tz v"pitche teshuba" ushear acharonim.

clarification.explanation: A dish containing no meat at all, but cooked in a pot that was used for meat (even if the pot was used for meat that very same day) — one may eat milk right after it immediately, without even needing to wash hands or rinse the mouth. Even if the pot was not thoroughly cleaned of meat-dish residue, one may still eat milk immediately. Nevertheless, if the pot was not properly cleaned, it is proper (out of caution) to require washing hands, rinsing, and mouth-rinsing — and then eat the milk immediately. All this applies only when there is a nullification measure (sixty) in the dish against the meat residue in the pot; but if there is not sixty against the meat residue, washing and rinsing alone do not suffice, and one must also wait at least one hour. One who is stringent to wait six hours even in this case is blessed.
takeaways: A pareve dish cooked in a meat pot (even used that same day) may be followed immediately by milk with no waiting at all, provided there is sixty against the meat residue in the pot.
If there is no sixty against the residue, one must wait at least one hour between the meat and the milk.

paragraphs: Akal betzim shennotenim biqdera sheyyesh bah besar chammin shel shabbat, vesudarim otah al hakkissuy shel haqqedera missabib, umitbashshelim mechom haqqedera shehi al haesh sheyyesh bah basar-chammin en tzarik lehamtin shesh shaot, veen tzarik hadacha veqinnucha: vehammachmir laasot hadacha veqinnucha bazeh, tabo alayv habberaka.

clarification.explanation: Eggs placed around the lid of a pot containing Sabbath meat stew, cooking from the pot's heat — one need not wait six hours (between meat and milk) after eating them, nor is rinsing and mouth-rinsing required (before eating milk). One who is stringent to rinse and mouth-rinse anyway is blessed.
takeaways: Eggs cooked by the heat of a Sabbath meat-stew pot do not have the law of meat: no six-hour wait afterward, and no rinsing or mouth-rinsing required.
One who is stringent about rinsing and mouth-rinsing anyway is blessed.

paragraphs: Akal chalab, muttar leekol acharayv basar miyyad, ak tzarik leqanneach piv yapeh bappat sheyyilasennu veyiblaennu, achar kak yedichennu bemayim yapeh, veachar kak yirchatz yadayv yapeh bemayim, veaz yokal habbasar miyyad.vaapillu im akal bemazleg, tzarik sheyyirchatz yadayv. unetilat yadayim zo shehi ben akilat chalab laakilat basar, tzarik shettihyeh letok keli, kedin mayim acharonim, kemo shekkatab maran za"l beorach-chayyim. veayyen "shiyyure beraka", avvat yt. veim en lo mayim, muttar lirchotz bishar mashqim bishat haddechaq, ukemo shekkatab "shiyyure beraka", avvat tz. vaapillu im rotzeh leekol besar op achar hechalab, tzarik qinnucha vahadachat peh unetilat-yadayim , vekannizkar b"bet yosep" , orach chayyim. veim en lo pat leqanneach bo piv, yukal leqanneach bishar perot, chutz miqqimcha vetamre veyarqa. vetzarik leqanneach techilla bepat, veachar kak yadicha bemayim ubediabad im hedicha veachar kak qnch en lachush veayyen" shiyyure beraka",ot k. veken im laas upalat velo bala, mehanne bediabad, abal lekattechilla vadday tzarik libloa, ubelav haki ikka issura biplita mishshum hepsed okalin, ukemo shekkatab b"pitche -teshuba", seip qatan h.

clarification.explanation: One who ate milk may eat meat immediately afterward, but must rinse his mouth thoroughly with bread (chewing bread and swallowing it), then rinse the mouth thoroughly with water, and afterward wash his hands thoroughly with water — and only then eat the meat immediately. Even if he ate the milk with a fork (without touching it with his hands), he must still wash his hands. This hand-washing between eating milk and meat must be done into a vessel, following the law of "final waters." If he has no water, in a pressing situation he may wash with other beverages. Even if one wants to eat fowl meat after milk, rinsing, mouth-rinsing, and hand-washing are required. If he has no bread to rinse with, he may rinse with other fruits (except flour, dates, and vegetables). One should rinse first with bread and only afterward rinse with water — but after the fact, if he rinsed with water before rinsing with bread, there is no concern. Likewise, if he chewed food and also spat it out without swallowing, this suffices after the fact (like rinsing), but as the primary practice one should swallow rather than spit it out, since there is also an issue of wasting food in spitting it out.
takeaways: The transition from milk to meat is easier than from meat to milk — it requires no hour-long waiting, only rinsing with bread, mouth-rinsing with water, and hand-washing (even if eaten with a fork).

paragraphs: Kol zeh shekkatabnu - beokel chalab qodem habbasar, abal beokel gebina, ap-al-gab demin shurat-haddin saggi beqinnucha vahadacha unetilat-yadayim kede leekol habbasar miyyad, mikkol maqom kebar nahagu lishhot zeman benehem: veyesh nohagim lishhot shaa achat, vegam sheyyihyeh bisuda acheret: veyesh shohin shelosh shaot. veharbeh gedole yisrael nahagu lehachmir shesh shaot, ukemo shekkatab haggaon chida" za"l b"shiyyure-beraka", avvat yg. upoh irenu bagdad morin kak: im hi gebina qasha sheabar aleha shishsha chodashim o yoter shohin shesh shaot, veim lo aberu aleha shishsha chodashim, mamtin shaa achat lekol chodesh echad: sheim abar chodesh mamtin shaa veim shene chodashim mamtin shette shaot, veken al zo hadderek. veharab haggaon morenu rabbi manni nr"v heid, deen minhagam beir haqqodesh yerushalayim t"v lehamtin achar gebina kelum ben chadasha, ben yeshana. veda, dehannohagim lehamtin bigbina, hu apillu shelloqeh o tzeluya. uminhag rabbenu haari"y za"l machmir beyoter dekol oto yom sheokel gebina eno okel basar: ashrayv veashre chelqo.

clarification.explanation: Everything stated so far concerns one who eats milk before meat. But one who eats cheese — although by strict law rinsing, mouth-rinsing, and hand-washing suffice to eat meat immediately afterward — the custom has nevertheless developed to wait some time between eating cheese and meat: some are accustomed to wait one hour and do so at a separate meal, and some wait three hours. Many of the great authorities of Israel were accustomed to be stringent and wait a full six hours, as the Chida wrote. In Baghdad the custom was: if the cheese is hard and six months or more have passed since it was made, one waits six hours; and if less than six months have passed, one waits one hour for each month — that is, one month, one hour; two months, two hours, and so on. In Jerusalem, by contrast, the custom was not to wait at all after cheese, whether new or old. One should know that those accustomed to wait after cheese are careful about this even if the cheese was cooked or roasted. And the custom of the Arizal was to be even more stringent: on the entire day he ate cheese, he would not eat meat at all — fortunate is one who follows this practice.
takeaways: After cheese (unlike ordinary milk), customs of waiting vary — from one hour to six hours, depending on the cheese's hardness and age, and on local custom.
The Arizal's custom of avoiding meat entirely on the day cheese was eaten is considered a special piety.

paragraphs: Haokel kechal, tzarik lehamtin shesh shaot kede leekol chalab: vehu haddin im okel kechal achar chalab, name dino keokel basar achar chalab.

clarification.explanation: One who eats the milk gland must wait six hours before eating milk, and likewise the law of one who eats the gland after milk — this is considered like the law of eating meat after milk.
takeaways: Eating the gland requires a six-hour wait before milk; but the gland after milk has the law of meat after milk — rinsing, mouth-rinsing, and hand-washing, without a six-hour wait.

paragraphs: En lasim issa bechalab, ella im ken shinna tzurat happat veim abar veapa belo shinnuy im eno dabar muat kede akila bebat achat, hakkol asur, velo yoil shinnuy achar apiyya, velo yoil lechalleqo libne adam harbeh leakelo bo bayyom bimhera, yaan shekkebar neesar miggezerat chaza"l. upoh irenu osin "sambusaq" (kisane batzeq memulla) shemmemalleim oto bigbina, veen osin bo shinnuy min simbusek hammulla beluzim vesukkar vaayin b"tiperet adam" sheqqiyyem hamminhag hazzeh: abal issa shellashin otah bechema o bechalab, veosin otah mine–mezonot nohagim poh irenu leshannot tzurat happat, apillu im osim meat kede akila achat: uminhag yapeh hu. vead poh irenu y", im osim pat bechalab kede limkor debar yom beyomo, veosim harbeh vegam ellu osin tzurato meshunneh, shehu noda venikkar lekol shehu shel chalab: ak da aqa, ki mhry"t za"l oser beosin limkor apillu al yede shinnuy, dechayeshinan laorechin: vaayin "peri chadash" v"chavvot- daat" shehiskimu ken. venireh li deyesh lehamlitz baadam: mishshum dezeh happat sheosin bechema, nirgash min harecha shello, veyesh kan kamma sepeqot dmhry"t lo asar bikhay gavna denikkar min harecha. vaayin leharab "mizmor ledavid" za"l shekkatab, beir moladto, shehi ir gedola shel chakamim vesoperim, nahagu hetter limkor bachanut vekatab taam hahetter, mishshum denakerim berecha vetaam, ayyen sham. vaayin "peri-toar" siman tzz, seip qatan g, mah shekkatab behetter hammeker mishshum sepeq-sepeqa, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: One should not put dough in milk (and bake bread from it) unless the ordinary bread's shape is changed, so it is recognizable as dairy bread and people do not come to eat it by mistake with meat. One who transgressed and baked without changing the shape — if it is not a small quantity eaten all at once, all the bread is forbidden, and there is no benefit in changing the shape after baking, nor any benefit in dividing the bread among several people to eat it quickly, since it has already been forbidden by the Sages' decree. In Baghdad it is customary to make "sambusak" (stuffed dough pastries) filled with cheese without changing their shape from other sambusak filled with nuts and sugar — and this custom is also supported by "Tiferet Adam." But dough kneaded with butter or milk made into cake-type pastries — the Baghdad custom is to change the bread's shape, even when making a small quantity for a single serving — and this is a fine custom. In Baghdad it was also customary, when making dairy bread for daily sale, to make it in a large quantity and in an unusual shape recognizable to all as dairy — but some hold (such as the Maharit) that it is forbidden to do this for sale even with a changed shape, out of concern that guests might not know and stumble. The Ben Ish Chai proposes a defense of the custom: since bread made with butter is recognizable by its smell, there is room to say the Maharit did not forbid it in a case where it is also recognizable by smell — and other authorities likewise wrote that in their locale the custom was to permit selling it in a shop, since it is recognizable by smell and taste.
takeaways: It is forbidden to bake bread with milk unless its shape is changed to be recognizable as dairy — if not changed and it is not a small quantity, all the bread is forbidden with no remedy after baking.
Regarding selling dairy bread in a shop, there is a dispute — some forbid out of concern for guests, and some permit since the smell and taste identify it as dairy.
